label: S0008
statement: statement: For every finite Boolean language F subseteq {0,1}^N with k=|F| and every cut t in {0,...,N}, the number D_t(F) of distinct residuals R_u={z in {0,1}^{N-t}: uz in F} over length-t prefixes satisfies D_t(F) <= k+1. Proof: A nonempty residual R_u contains some suffix z, and then uz is an element of F whose length-t prefix is u. Thus every prefix u with nonempty residual is a length-t prefix of at least one word of F. There are at most k such prefixes, hence at most k distinct nonempty residuals. There is at most one additional residual, the empty set, so D_t(F)<=k+1. This includes F=empty and cuts t=0,N. Scope: fixed-length finite Boolean languages; state-count bound only, with no circuit/update-time implication.

label: S0009
statement: statement: For every N>=1, F subseteq {0,1}^N, and cut 0<=t<=N, let D_t(F) be the number of distinct residuals R_u={z in {0,1}^{N-t}: uz in F}. Then D_t(F)<=min(2^t, 2^{N-t}, |F|+1). Proof: There are 2^t length-t prefixes, so at most 2^t residuals. Every residual is a subset of the 2^{N-t} suffixes, but this alone gives 2^{2^{N-t}} possible sets; instead, each nonempty residual contains a suffix and therefore corresponds to at least one word uz in F. Distinct nonempty residuals must arise from distinct prefixes, and each such prefix contains at least one distinct word of F, so there are at most min(2^t,|F|) nonempty residuals. There is at most one empty residual. Thus D_t(F)<=min(2^t,|F|)+1. Also, each residual is a subset of F's suffix set, whose size is at most |F|, so this does not establish the stated 2^{N-t} term; the valid conclusion is D_t(F)<=min(2^t,|F|)+1. Scope: fixed-length finite Boolean languages; this is a state-count upper bound and implies no update-time or circuit-size bound.

label: S0011
statement:
statement_start: For every finite Boolean language F subseteq {0,1}^N and every deterministic exact one-pass decider M, the layered quotient by equal continuation behavior is a well-defined exact machine with D_t(F) states at cut t; its transitions are well-defined and it is minimal at each cut.
proof: For each t-prefix u define R_u={z in {0,1}^{N-t}: uz in F}. At layer t identify u,v iff R_u=R_v. If R_u=R_v, then for either next bit b and every suffix z of length N-t-1, z∈R_{ub} iff bz∈R_u iff bz∈R_v iff z∈R_{vb}; hence R_{ub}=R_{vb}, so the transition on b is well-defined on equivalence classes. The initial class is R_empty=F. At layer N, the sole suffix is empty and acceptance is its membership in R_u, which equals the definition of F, proving exactness. label: S0012
statement:
statement_start: Let M be a deterministic exact one-pass decider for F subseteq {0,1}^N with state sets Q_t, transitions δ_t, and residual map π_t(q) equal to the continuation language after any prefix reaching q. If π_t and π_{t+1} have Boolean circuit implementations, then the canonical residual transition τ_t satisfies π_{t+1}∘δ_t(·,b)=τ_t(π_t(·),b), and has circuit size at most size(π_{t+1})+size(δ_t)+size(π_t) plus wire overhead.
proof: For any reachable state q after prefix u of length t, define π_t(q)=R_u={z∈{0,1}^{N-t}:uz∈F}. This is well-defined: if two prefixes u,v reach the same state q, determinism gives identical accept/reject outcomes on every common continuation z, so R_u=R_v. Define τ_t(R,b) by τ_t(R,b)={z:bz∈R}. Then for every such q and every suffix z, z∈π_{t+1}(δ_t(q,b)) iff the machine accepts after prefix ub followed by z iff bz∈π_t(q), iff z∈τ_t(π_t(q),b). Thus the function identity holds on every reachable q. To implement the induced update on encoded residual labels, compute π_t(q), apply the original δ_t(q,b) while retaining q, then compute π_{t+1} of the resulting state; alternatively a circuit for τ_t can be composed directly with π_t. Circuit composition gives an implementation size at most size(π_t)+size(τ_t)+O(1), while τ_t equals the stated π_{t+1}∘δ_t factorization on reachable states and therefore can be implemented by that composition with size at most size(π_{t+1})+size(δ_t)+O(1). This is a conditional simulation theorem; without circuit bounds for π_t and π_{t+1}, it implies no small update cost.
scope: Finite-horizon exact deterministic streaming machines. State encodings may be nonlinear and time-dependent, but the result assumes Boolean circuits for the residual extraction maps on reachable states. It gives no lower bound and no representation of arbitrary machines as a GF(p)-linear kernel.

label: S0013
statement:
statement_start: For a deterministic exact one-pass machine M for F⊆{0,1}^N, the residual transition T_t(R,b)={z:bz∈R} is well-defined on reachable residuals and agrees with the residual of the successor machine state.
proof: Let Q_t be machine states reachable after t bits, δ_t its transition, and let π_t(q) be the set of suffixes accepted from q. First, π_t is well-defined: if prefixes u,v reach the same q, determinism implies identical acceptance on every common suffix z, so R_u=R_v. For any reachable q and bit b, define R=π_t(q). For each z∈{0,1}^{N-t-1}, z∈π_{t+1}(δ_t(q,b)) iff the machine accepts from q on input bz iff bz∈R iff z∈T_t(R,b), where T_t(R,b):={z:bz∈R}. Thus π_{t+1}(δ_t(q,b))=T_t(π_t(q),b). In particular, if two reachable states q,q′ have the same residual R, their successor states under b have the same residual T_t(R,b); hence T_t is a well-defined function on the set of reachable residuals.
scope: Finite-horizon deterministic exact streaming machines. This proves existence and correctness of the induced transition on reachable residuals. It makes no circuit-size or update-time claim: implementations of π_t on machine-state inputs do not supply an inverse encoding or circuit on residual encodings. No general lower bound or P vs NP consequence.

statement:
statement_start: For every N≥1, every F⊆{0,1}^N, and every cut 0≤t<N, encode each residual R⊆{0,1}^{N−t} by its incidence vector v_R∈{0,1}^{2^{N−t}}, indexed lexicographically by suffixes. The residual transition T_t(R,b)={z:bz∈R} is implemented by a coordinate projection using no Boolean gates, with output width 2^{N−t−1}.
proof: Let input coordinates be indexed by all suffixes w∈{0,1}^{N−t}, and set (v_R)_w=1 iff w∈R. For each z∈{0,1}^{N−t−1}, define y_z=(v_R)_{bz}. Then y_z=1 iff bz∈R, iff z∈T_t(R,b), so y is exactly the incidence vector of the successor residual. Each output bit copies one input bit, hence the update is a coordinate projection and uses zero Boolean gates when wires and coordinate selection are free. The encoding width is 2^{N−t}; this gives no succinct streaming machine or polynomial-resource algorithm.

label: S0025
statement: statement_start: Residual count bound with proof: Let N>=1, F subseteq {0,1}^N, and 0<=t<=N. For each length-t prefix u let R_u={z in {0,1}^{N-t}: uz in F}, and let D_t(F) count distinct residuals. Then D_t(F)<=min(2^t,|F|)+1.

structure.evidence: Repair of refuted step S0009. The original claim D_t(F) <= min(2^t, 2^{N-t}, |F|+1) was refuted by counterexample N=5,t=3 where D_3(F)=8 but 2^{N-t}=4. Corrected proof: At most 2^t prefixes exist. For each distinct nonempty residual choose one inducing prefix u and one suffix z in it; the word uz belongs to F. Distinct residuals have distinct chosen prefixes, so chosen words are distinct; thus nonempty residuals <= |F|. At most one empty residual. Therefore D_t(F) <= min(2^t, |F|) + 1. The 2^{2^{N-t}} bound from subset counting is vacuous; the |F|+1 bound is the nontrivial one.

label: S0029
statement: For every N>=1, F subseteq {0,1}^N, and 0<=t<=N, consider a deterministic layered machine that reads N bits and decides membership in F. If two length-t prefixes u,v have distinct residuals R_u={z in {0,1}^{N-t}:uz in F} and R_v={z in {0,1}^{N-t}:vz in F}, then the machine reaches different states after u and v. Proof: Since the residuals differ, choose a suffix z in their symmetric difference. If the machine reached the same state after u and v, determinism would make its future computation on the common suffix z identical, hence its final acceptance decisions on uz and vz would agree. But exactly one of uz,vz belongs to F, contradicting that the machine decides F. Therefore the number of reachable states at layer t is at least D_t(F). Conversely, a machine with one state per distinct residual is obtained by transitioning R to R_b={z:bz in R} on bit b, and accepting at the final layer iff the residual contains the empty string; induction shows it decides F. Thus the minimum number of reachable states at layer t is exactly D_t(F).

structure.evidence: Direct general proof for fixed-length Boolean languages. Scope is state count only; it gives no transition circuit-size or update-time lower bound.

label: S0031
statement: Let N>=1, F⊆{0,1}^N, and 0≤t<N. For each residual R at layer t define T_b(R)={z∈{0,1}^{N−t−1}: bz∈R}, for b∈{0,1}. Then T_0(R) and T_1(R) are disjoint and their union is {z: 0z∈R or 1z∈R}; each is uniquely determined by R and b. Proof: Every y∈R has a unique decomposition y=bz by its first bit and remaining suffix, so z belongs to exactly one of the two sets. Conversely, membership z∈T_b(R) means bz∈R by definition. Thus the successor residuals partition the tails represented in R and do not depend on which prefix induced R. This proves the canonical residual automaton has well-defined transitions. It gives no Boolean gate bound for implementing those transitions.

label: S0032
statement: Let F={w_1,...,w_B} be a list of distinct words in {0,1}^N. There is a layered deterministic machine deciding membership in F with B survivor bits and at most B+1 fan-in-two gates per transition layer. Initialize s_j=1. At layer t, on input b, set s'_j=s_j AND [b=w_j[t]]. Accept after N bits iff some s_j=1. Proof: Inductively, after prefix u, s_j=1 iff u agrees with the first |u| bits of w_j. This is true initially; the update preserves the invariant exactly when the next bit matches. Thus after N bits a survivor exists iff the input is in F. Each coordinate update takes one AND with a shared literal b or NOT b; computing NOT b once gives at most B+1 gates. For B>=1 the final OR takes at most B-1 gates. Scope: explicit listed languages, with layer-specific nonuniform transitions; no compact representation or MCSP bound follows.

statement:
statement: For m>=1 and a Boolean function f:{0,1}^m->{0,1} with t>=1 accepting inputs, a DNF using one minterm for each accepting input computes f with at most tm-1 binary AND/OR gates when input negations are free; if NOT gates are charged but shared, at most tm-1+m gates suffice.
proof: For each accepting input a, form the conjunction of its m literals, using m-1 binary AND gates (for m=1 this is one literal and uses zero). OR the t conjunctions using t-1 binary OR gates. The resulting DNF is true exactly on the accepting inputs. Its AND/OR cost is t(m-1)+(t-1)=tm-1. With charged NOT gates, negate each input variable that occurs negatively in any minterm once and share that output; there are at most m such variables, adding at most m gates.

Per-restriction gate consumption alone does not control repeated use of shared gates.

statement: statement: For every n>=1, every A subseteq {0,1}^n, and every q in {0,...,n}, the average over uniformly chosen prefixes p in {0,1}^q of |{x in A: x_1...x_q=p}| equals |A|/2^q. statement: statement: For every finite A subseteq {0,1}^n and q in {0,...,n}, if R_p=|{x in A:x_1...x_q=p}| for p in {0,1}^q, then 2^{-q} sum_p R_p^2 = 2^{-q}|{(x,y) in A^2: x_1...x_q=y_1...y_q}|. Proof: expand R_p^2 as sum over ordered pairs (x,y) in A^2 of the indicator that both have prefix p; summing over p counts the pair once if their prefixes agree and zero otherwise. Dividing by 2^q gives the identity. This expresses the second moment as a collision statistic and is sensitive to prefix clustering, unlike the first moment.

statement: statement: For integers K,B>=1 and 0<=t<=KB, among all integer vectors (R_1,...,R_K) with 0<=R_i<=B and sum_i R_i=t, the minimum of sum_i R_i^2 is (K-v)u^2+v(u+1)^2 where t=uK+v, 0<=v<K; the maximum is aB^2+r^2 where t=aB+r, 0<=r<B. Proof: for the minimum, if R_i>=R_j+2, replacing (R_i,R_j) by (R_i-1,R_j+1) changes the sum by -2(R_i-R_j)+2<0, so at a minimum all entries differ by at most one; the fixed sum forces v entries u+1 and K-v entries u. For the maximum, if 0<R_j<=R_i<B, moving one unit from j to i changes the sum by 2(R_i-R_j)+2>0; hence at a maximum at most one entry is strictly between 0 and B, and all others are 0 or B; the fixed sum forces a entries B, one entry r if r>0, and the rest 0. These vectors are feasible since t<=KB.

label: S0006
statement: statement: For integers m>=1 and s>=0, the number of Boolean functions on m inputs computable by circuits with at most s ordered fan-in-2 gates over a basis of at most 16 Boolean operations is at most (m+s)(16(m+s)^2)^s (interpreting the s=0 case directly). Proof: Pad a circuit with unused gates to exactly s gates. In an ordered description, each gate chooses one of at most 16 operations and an ordered pair of predecessors among at most m+s available input or gate wires, giving at most 16(m+s)^2 choices. The output chooses one of at most m+s wires. Thus the number of descriptions is at most (m+s)(16(m+s)^2)^s, and each computes at most one Boolean function, so the number of distinct functions is no larger.

statement: statement: Lemma (cofactor gate removal with free constants). For any fan-in-2 Boolean circuit C with s gates, any set I of input variables, and any assignment a in {0,1}^I, let E_a be the gates whose computed functions become constant after fixing I=a. Then C restricted by I=a has a fan-in-2 circuit of size at most s-|E_a|. Proof: traverse C in topological order, replace every gate in E_a by its constant value under the restriction, and feed that value to every consumer. Retain the other gates. The output is unchanged and each gate in E_a is removed once, including when it has multiple consumers. Consequently, for uniform a, E_a's average size is 2^{-|I|} sum_g |{a : gate g becomes constant under I=a}|.

structure.gap: This lemma does not establish a lower bound on the aggregate number of gates that become constant for restrictions of MCSP[m^c]. The remaining GE-3 obstacle is relating that statistic to the MCSP circuit's total size under arbitrary sharing.

For any fan-in-2 Boolean circuit C with s gates, any set I of input variables, and any assignment a in {0,1}^I, let E_a be the gates whose computed functions become constant after fixing I=a. Then C restricted by I=a has a fan-in-2 circuit of size at most s-|E_a|. Proof: traverse C in topological order, replace every gate in E_a by its constant value under the restriction, and feed that value to every consumer. Retain the other gates. The output is unchanged and each gate in E_a is removed once, including when it has multiple consumers. Consequently, for uniform a, E_a's average size is 2^{-|I|} sum_g |{a : gate g becomes constant under I=a}|.

label: S0009
statement: statement: Lemma (restriction-independent gates survive). Let C be a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit on variables X∪Y, and let g be a gate whose computed Boolean function depends only on Y. For every assignment a to X, the gate function after restricting X=a is the same function h(Y). If h is nonconstant, g remains nonconstant. Proof: write the gate function as h(Y). Substitution of a for X changes no argument of h, so the restricted gate still computes h(Y). Since h is nonconstant, it remains nonconstant for every a.

label: S0010
statement: statement: Lemma (survival probability from one nonconstant cofactor). Let C be a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit with s gates on disjoint variable sets X∪Y, |X|=r. For each gate g and assignment a∈{0,1}^X, let g_a be its restricted Boolean function on Y. If N gates have at least one assignment a for which g_a is nonconstant, then under uniform a the expected number of nonconstant restricted gate functions is at least N/2^r. Proof: each counted gate has at least one surviving restriction among 2^r equally likely assignments, so its survival probability is at least 2^-r. The expected surviving-gate count is the sum of these indicator probabilities. No independence is required, and arbitrary fan-out does not affect the gate count.

label: S0011
statement:
statement: Lemma (survival of Y-only gates under X-restriction). Let C be a Boolean circuit on disjoint input sets X and Y, and let H be any set of gates whose computed functions are nonconstant and depend only on Y. For every assignment a to X, every gate in H computes the same nonconstant function of Y in C|_{X=a}; hence none is removed when replacing constant gates, and |C|−|E_a|≥|H|, where E_a is the set of gates that become constant after restriction. Proof: each gate g∈H computes h_g(Y) before restriction, with no dependence on X. Substituting X=a therefore leaves its function exactly h_g(Y). Since h_g is nonconstant, g is not in E_a. Thus H∩E_a=∅, so |E_a|≤|C|−|H| and the inequality follows. This holds pointwise for every a, even with arbitrary fan-out and shared gates.
proof: For each g in H, its Boolean function is h_g(Y), independent of X and nonconstant. Substituting any assignment a for X leaves h_g(Y) unchanged, so g does not become constant. Therefore H is disjoint from E_a and |E_a|≤|C|−|H|.

label: S0012
statement:
statement: Lemma (cofactor survival for Y-dependent gates). Let X,Y be disjoint Boolean input sets with |X|=q, and let f:{0,1}^X×{0,1}^Y->{0,1} depend on at least one Y input. For uniform a∈{0,1}^X, Pr[f(a,·) is nonconstant]≥2^{-q}. Proof: Y-dependence gives x*, y,y' with f(x*,y)≠f(x*,y'); hence the cofactor at x* is nonconstant, and a=x* has probability 2^{-q}. Sharpness: f(X,y)=1[X=x*]∧y has exactly one surviving cofactor. For any h such gate functions in a circuit, linearity of expectation gives expected at least h2^{-q} nonconstant gate cofactors, irrespective of shared fan-out.
proof: For each function choose a witnessing assignment x* and witnessing Y inputs y,y'. The random restriction equals x* with probability 2^{-q}, which preserves a nonconstant cofactor. Summing the survival indicators over gates and applying linearity of expectation gives the aggregate expectation; no independence is needed.

label: S0013
statement:
statement: Lemma (support-sensitive cofactor survival). Let C be a Boolean circuit on disjoint input sets X and Y, and for each gate g let f_g(X,Y) be its computed Boolean function. Let d_g be the number of coordinates of X on which f_g actually depends. If f_g depends on at least one coordinate of Y, then for a uniform a in {0,1}^X, Pr[f_g(a,·) is nonconstant] >= 2^{-d_g}. Consequently, for any set H of gates whose functions depend on Y, the expected number of gates in H with nonconstant cofactors is at least sum_{g in H} 2^{-d_g}.
proof: Fix g in H. Since f_g depends on Y, there are x*, y, y' with f_g(x*,y) != f_g(x*,y'). Fix the d_g coordinates in the X-support of f_g to their values in x*. For every assignment to the remaining X coordinates, the two evaluations still differ because f_g is independent of those coordinates. Thus at least a 2^{-d_g} fraction of all assignments to X give a nonconstant Y-cofactor. Summing the survival indicators over H and taking expectations proves the aggregate inequality by linearity of expectation; no independence between gates is needed. The bound is sharp: f(X,y)=1[X|_S=x*] AND y, where |S|=d, has a nonconstant cofactor on exactly one assignment to S.

label: S0014
statement: statement: Sensitivity witness lemma. Let X,Y be finite nonempty sets and f:X×Y→{0,1}. For y0,y1∈Y, define D={x∈X:f(x,y0)≠f(x,y1)}. For each x∈X, call the restricted gate f(x,·) surviving if it is nonconstant on Y. Then at least |D| of the |X| restrictions survive. Proof: for every x∈D the two values f(x,y0),f(x,y1) differ, so f(x,·) takes both Boolean values and is nonconstant. Thus D is contained in the set of surviving restrictions, giving the cardinality inequality. In uniform form, survival probability is at least |D|/|X|.

label: S0015
statement: statement: Averaged cofactor-survival bound. Let X,Y be finite nonempty sets and let f_1,...,f_s:X×Y→{0,1}. For each i,x let p_i(x)=|{y∈Y:f_i(x,y)=1}|/|Y|, and let S(x)=|{i:y↦f_i(x,y) is nonconstant}|. Then Σ_{x∈X}S(x) ≥ Σ_{x∈X}Σ_{i=1}^s 2p_i(x)(1-p_i(x)). Proof: choose independent uniform y0,y1∈Y. For each fixed x,i, the probability f_i(x,y0)≠f_i(x,y1) is p_i(x)(1-p_i(x))+(1-p_i(x))p_i(x)=2p_i(x)(1-p_i(x)). Whenever this disagreement occurs, the cofactor y↦f_i(x,y) is nonconstant. Thus pointwise the number of disagreeing (x,i) pairs is at most Σ_x S(x). Take expectation and use linearity of expectation to obtain the inequality.

label: S0023
statement:
statement: Lemma (support-sensitive cofactor survival). Let X and Y be disjoint finite sets of Boolean variables and let f:{0,1}^X×{0,1}^Y→{0,1}. Let d be the number of X-coordinates on which f essentially depends. If f depends on at least one Y-coordinate, then for uniform a∈{0,1}^X, Pr[f(a,·) is nonconstant]≥2^{-d}. Proof: Since f depends on Y, there are x*∈{0,1}^X and y,y'∈{0,1}^Y such that f(x*,y)≠f(x*,y'). Let S⊆X be the set of essential X-coordinates, so |S|=d. For every a agreeing with x* on S, f(a,y)=f(x*,y) and f(a,y')=f(x*,y'), because f is independent of X\S. Hence each such a gives a nonconstant Y-cofactor. Exactly 2^{|X|-d} assignments agree on S, so the probability is at least 2^{-d}. The bound is attained, for d≥0, by f(X,y)=1[X|_S=x*|_S]∧y when Y has a designated bit y (and ignores its other bits): precisely one assignment to S gives a nonconstant cofactor, so the probability is 2^{-d}.
evidence: Complete finite-set argument given in the statement. The independent bounded enumeration cm-c76d2cc7e2024477 checked all functions with |X|≤3 and |Y|=1 (2, 12, 240, and 65,280 Y-dependent functions at |X|=0,1,2,3) and found no counterexample; this computation is corroboration only, not the general proof.

label: S0024
statement:
statement: Lemma (support bounds nonconstant output cofactors). Let X,Y be disjoint finite Boolean variable sets, r=|X|, and f:{0,1}^X×{0,1}^Y→{0,1} have support size t=|{(x,y):f(x,y)=1}|. Let A={a∈{0,1}^X : f(a,·) is nonconstant}. Then |A|≤min(2^r,t), so for uniform a, Pr[f(a,·) is nonconstant]≤min(1,t/2^r). If f is the output of any fan-in-2 circuit, this is also an upper bound on the probability that its output gate remains nonconstant after restricting X.
proof: For every a∈A, nonconstancy of f(a,·) implies there exists y_a with f(a,y_a)=1. The sets {(a,y): y∈{0,1}^Y} for distinct a are disjoint, so choosing one such positive input per a injects A into supp(f); hence |A|≤t. Trivially |A|≤2^r. Dividing by 2^r proves the probability bound. The circuit statement follows because its output gate computes exactly f, and a gate remains nonconstant precisely when its restricted output function is nonconstant.

label: S0025
statement:
statement: Lemma (aggregate cofactor-survival bound for circuit gates). Let C be a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit with gate set G on disjoint finite Boolean input sets X and Y, with |X|=r. For each gate g, let f_g:{0,1}^X×{0,1}^Y→{0,1} be its computed function and let t_g=|supp(f_g)|. For a∈{0,1}^X, let I_g(a)=1 iff f_g(a,·) is nonconstant. Then Σ_a Σ_{g∈G} I_g(a) ≤ Σ_{g∈G} min(2^r,t_g). Equivalently, for uniform a, the expected number of nonconstant gate cofactors is at most 2^-r Σ_g min(2^r,t_g). This holds with arbitrary fan-out and gate sharing.
proof: Fix g. Define A_g={a∈{0,1}^X:f_g(a,·) is nonconstant}. For each a∈A_g, nonconstancy implies there is y_a with f_g(a,y_a)=1. The X-fibers for distinct a are disjoint, so the selected satisfying inputs (a,y_a) are distinct members of supp(f_g). Thus |A_g|≤t_g. Also |A_g|≤2^r, hence |A_g|≤min(2^r,t_g). Summing this inequality over the finite gate set G gives Σ_a Σ_g I_g(a)=Σ_g |A_g|≤Σ_g min(2^r,t_g). Dividing by 2^r gives the expectation formula. The proof counts gates individually and makes no independence assumption, so sharing and fan-out do not affect it.

statement:
statement: Lemma (support-weighted expected retained gates). Let C be a Boolean circuit and let X,Y be disjoint input sets. For each gate g, write f_g(X,Y) for its computed function, d_g for the number of X-coordinates in its actual support, and H for any set of gates whose functions depend on at least one Y-coordinate. Under a uniform assignment a to X, the expected number of gates in H whose restricted functions f_g(a,·) are nonconstant is at least Σ_{g∈H}2^{-d_g}. Proof: Fix g∈H. Since f_g depends on Y, choose x*, y, y′ with f_g(x*,y)≠f_g(x*,y′). Fix the d_g support coordinates of X to their values in x*. For every completion on the other X-coordinates, f_g is unchanged because it is independent of those coordinates; thus the same y,y′ witness a nonconstant cofactor. Exactly 2^{|X|-d_g} assignments extend this fixing, so the survival probability is at least 2^{-d_g}. Sum the indicator variables for g∈H and use linearity of expectation; no independence assumption is needed. The bound is sharp for an individual gate, e.g. f(X,y)=1[X|_S=x*]∧y with |S|=d_g.
proof: As in the statement: each gate has at least 2^{|X|-d_g} surviving assignments, hence survival probability at least 2^{-d_g}; summing expectations proves the result.

label: S0027
statement:
statement: For a Boolean function f:{0,1}^X x {0,1}^Y -> {0,1}, let S be its actual X-support and A={a in {0,1}^S : f(a,.) is nonconstant}. Under a uniform assignment to X, the probability that the restricted cofactor on Y is nonconstant is exactly |A|/2^|S|. In particular, if f depends on Y then this probability is at least 2^-|S|, and this lower bound is sharp.
proof: Because f is independent of every coordinate in X\S, the restricted function f(x,.) depends only on x|_S. For uniform x in {0,1}^X, x|_S is uniform on {0,1}^S. The event that f(x,.) is nonconstant is therefore exactly the event x|_S belongs to A, which has probability |A|/2^|S|. If f depends on Y, at least one cofactor is nonconstant: otherwise all cofactors would be constant, and since f is Y-dependent this would be impossible. Thus |A|>=1. Sharpness is witnessed by f(x,y)=1[x|_S=a*] AND y, for any a* in {0,1}^S, whose nonconstant-cofactor set is the singleton {a*}.

statement: Counting lemma: if m = s(2*ceil(log2(n+s))+2)+ceil(log2(n+s)) < 2^n then some n-input Boolean function has circuit size > s over {AND,OR,XOR,NOT}.

A witness must be produced within the one-pass update-time budget, and space bounds alone do not control that cost (spec note: only an update-time lower bound can establish the hypothesis). structure.lemma: Let L = ceil(log2(n+s)) and m = s(2L+2)+L. If m < 2^n, then some Boolean function on n inputs has circuit size > s over {AND, OR, XOR, NOT} (NOT counted as a gate). Proof: a circuit of size <= s is determined by an m-bit description (per gate: 2-bit op code and two operand indices of L bits each, plus an L-bit output index). The map from descriptions to truth tables therefore has image of size <= 2^m. There are 2^(2^n) n-variable functions, and 2^m < 2^(2^n) when m < 2^n, so by pigeonhole some function is not in the image. Folklore counting; not a new theorem.
structure.proved_step: Counting lemma: if m = s(2*ceil(log2(n+s))+2)+ceil(log2(n+s)) < 2^n then some n-input Boolean function has circuit size > s over {AND,OR,XOR,NOT}.

label: S0003
statement:
statement: Let N=2^n, L=ceil(log2(n+s)), m=s(2L+2)+L, and assume m < 2^n. Let R be the set of truth tables on n inputs of circuit size <= s over {AND,OR,XOR,NOT}, and let R_p be the set of length-p prefixes (fixed input order) of tables in R. Then (a) |R_p| <= 2^m for every p <= N; (b) some w in {0,1}^(m+1) is not in R_(m+1), and every table with prefix w has circuit size > s. Hence the minimal dead depth p* = min{p : R_p != {0,1}^p} satisfies p* <= m+1 = O(s log(n+s)).
proof: (a) R_p is the image of R under the prefix map pi_p, so |R_p| <= |R| <= 2^m by the encoding in S0001/S0002: each circuit of size <= s is described by s(2L+2)+L bits (2-bit opcode and two L-bit operands per gate, L-bit output index), and L = ceil(log2(n+s)) indexes all n+s nodes; dummy gates pad smaller circuits, so the description map is onto R. (b) m < 2^n gives m+1 <= N, so pi_(m+1) is defined. |{0,1}^(m+1)| = 2^(m+1) > 2^m >= |R_(m+1)|, so some w is missing. If f had prefix w and C(f) <= s, then f in R and w = pi_(m+1)(f) in R_(m+1), a contradiction. Scope: shrinks G0001 by locating the witness within m+1 stream positions; does NOT close G0001, since no update-time bound on deciding membership in R_p follows. Trivial counting bookkeeping, not progress toward P vs NP.

label: S0012
statement:
statement: Lemma (sorted-list prefix avoidance with logarithmic probes). Let D be a multiset of d Boolean strings of common length N, stored in lexicographically sorted order and available by random access. Put m=ceil(log2(max(1,d))). If N>=m+1, a prefix of length m+1 that is extended by no member of D can be constructed using O((m+1) log(d+1)) string probes and O(m+1) working bits. At each stage the strings matching the current prefix form a contiguous interval [a,b) in the sorted list. The two next-bit classes are contiguous subintervals; their sizes can be found by binary searching the boundary between 0 and 1. Choose the smaller class, ties to 0. After i choices, the live interval has size at most d/2^i by induction. At i=m+1 this is strictly less than 1, hence zero. Each boundary search uses O(log(d+1)) random-access probes, proving the stated bound.
evidence: Proof by interval contiguity of lexicographic order, binary search for the transition to next bit 1, and induction on live-interval size. This is a restricted data-access lemma; it does not close G0001 because circuit descriptions are not supplied as a sorted list with cheap random access.

label: S0013
statement: statement: Lemma (dynamic trie costs for prefix avoidance). Let D be a multiset of d Boolean strings of common length N, stored in a binary trie with a count at each node equal to the number of strings extending that node's prefix. Inserting or deleting one string takes O(N) time by changing the counts on its root-to-leaf path. Given this trie, an absent prefix of length m+1 can be found in O(m) time, where m=ceil(log2(max(1,d))), provided N>=m+1: at each level choose a child of minimum count, ties to 0. After i choices the live count is at most d/2^i by induction, so after m+1 choices it is less than 1 and hence zero. A trie for d strings of length N has O(dN) nodes in the worst case. Proof: each insertion/deletion visits exactly N+1 nodes; each query visits at most m+1 nodes and uses the stored exact counts; the halving induction proves the selected leaf prefix has count zero.

structure.lemma: Let f: {0,1}^N -> {0,1}, 0<t<N, M_t the 2^t x 2^(N-t) matrix M_t[a,b]=f(a,b), F any field, D_t = number of distinct rows of M_t. Then (i) rank_F(M_t) <= D_t; (ii) any deterministic streaming machine whose state after reading prefix a takes D_t distinct values (one per row class) with S state bits satisfies D_t <= 2^S; hence S >= log2 rank_F(M_t). Proof: (i) the rows span a space of dimension rank_F(M_t), and a spanning set can be chosen from the distinct rows, so rank <= D_t. (ii) rows with different contents must have different states, since their outputs differ on some suffix, so there are at least D_t distinct states and therefore at least ceil(log2 D_t) bits; by (i), D_t >= rank_F(M_t). Scope: exact, all N, all fields F; log-loss only (rank alone gives no bit lower bound); no claim of P != NP progress.

Conversely, the states can be taken to be the D_t distinct row classes, so D_t states suffice. This replaces the rank-based route: D_t is exact, not a log-loss proxy. statement:
statement: For finite D⊆{0,1}^S and c:D→{0,1}^H, a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit outputs c(x) on D and 0^H outside D, with O(S|D|+H|D|) gates.
proof: Build the binary prefix trie of D. Set the root indicator to 1; for each edge, AND the parent indicator with the corresponding input literal. Each leaf indicator is 1 exactly on its word. For each output bit, OR the leaf indicators whose correction has that bit set (use constant 0 if none). On D exactly one leaf is active; outside D none is active. The trie has at most S|D| edges and the output ORs use at most H|D| gates. For D=∅ use constant-zero outputs.

statement:
statement: For integers S,H≥0, finite D⊆{0,1}^S, and c:D→{0,1}^H with q=|c(D)|, there is a fan-in-2 Boolean circuit F that equals c on D and 0^H outside D, using at most S|D|+|D|+Hq gates, subject to constant and empty-operation conventions.
proof: Build the prefix trie of D, with one AND gate per edge to produce each leaf indicator; this costs at most S|D| gates. Partition the leaves by their correction vector. For each of the q nonempty groups, OR its leaf indicators, costing |D|-q gates total. For each output bit, OR the group indicators whose correction vector has that bit set, costing at most Hq gates. statement: For integers S,H>=0, finite D subseteq {0,1}^S, and c:D->{0,1}^H, write V=c(D). statement: In the fan-in-2 Boolean circuit model where NOT gates are counted and constants and wires are free, for finite D subset {0,1}^S and c:D->{0,1}^H, there is a circuit equal to c on D and 0^H outside D with at most S|D|+|D|-|c(D)|+sum_{v in c(D)}wt(v)+S gates. proof: Construction and gate accounting as stated; the S shared NOT gates supply all literals used by trie edges.

statement: statement: Let S,H>=0, D be a finite subset of {0,1}^S, c:D->{0,1}^H, V=c(D), and B(D)={i in {1,...,S}: there exists x in D with x_i=0}. In the fan-in-2 Boolean circuit model with NOT gates counted and constants and wires free, there is a circuit F:{0,1}^S->{0,1}^H equal to c on D and 0^H outside D with at most S|D|+|D|-|V|+sum_{v in V}wt(v)+|B(D)| gates. Proof: If D is empty, use constant-zero outputs. Otherwise form NOT(x_i) for each i in B(D), using |B(D)| gates. For every coordinate i not in B(D), all points of D have x_i=1, so any trie edge at coordinate i uses the positive literal; for i in B(D), either polarity is available. Build the prefix trie of D, with root indicator 1 and one AND gate for each nonempty-prefix edge, using at most S|D| gates. Group leaf indicators by their c-value; the |V| nonempty groups require |D|-|V| OR gates in total. For output coordinate b, OR the group indicators whose value v has v_b=1; this costs at most the number of such groups, so at most sum_v wt(v) gates over all coordinates. For x in D exactly its leaf and group are active, giving c(x); outside D no leaf is active, giving 0^H. Adding these costs proves the bound. Diagnostic: this is a finite-domain circuit upper bound and claims no P-vs-NP progress.

For every f on n>=1 variables: f has a DNF with |f^-1(1)| terms and a CNF with |f^-1(0)| clauses, so min(DNF terms, CNF clauses) <= 2^(n-1). Tight for parity_n: any term with k<n literals is satisfied by points of both parities, so it is not an implicant; every DNF for parity_n uses only full minterms and needs 2^(n-1) terms (dually for CNF). Consequence: the naive depth-2 size measure (terms or clauses) cannot exceed 2^(n-1), so a separation in K12-D2 needs a different measure (wires, fan-in, or a restricted class). This closes no obligation and is not P vs NP progress.
structure.proved_step: DEPTH-2 SIZE LEMMA: min(DNF terms, CNF clauses) <= 2^(n-1) for every f on n>=1 variables, tight at parity_n (proof in lemma field; checked by cm-depth2-size-verify)

label: S0009
statement: LEMMA R: Let w in Z^n with |w_i| <= M, t real, s = |supp w| >= 1. Let S contain each coordinate independently with probability p <= 1/8, z uniform on fixed coordinates. Then P[gate [w.x >= t] non-constant in x_S] <= C_M p sqrt(n), C_M = sqrt(2)(M/2+2)+4. Proof: j = |S cap supp|, W = sum over S of |w_i| <= M j, N = s - j. Given S the gate is non-constant iff X = sum over fixed support w_i z_i lies in a half-open window of length W, so j >= 1 is needed. Case 1<=j<=s/2: N >= s/2 >= 1, all fixed weights are nonzero integers, so Erdos-Littlewood-Offord (open intervals of length 2 contain at most binom(N, floor(N/2)) sums, and binom(N,floor(N/2))/2^N <= 1/sqrt(N)) gives P_z <= (Mj/2+2)/sqrt(s/2). With 1[j>=1] <= j and E j = ps, this part is <= sqrt(2)(M/2+2) p sqrt(s) <= sqrt(2)(M/2+2) p sqrt(n). Case j > s/2 (s >= 2, 4p <= 1/2): P <= binom(s, ceil(s/2)) p^{ceil(s/2)} <= (4p)^{s/2} <= 4p; for s = 1 it is p. Summing gives the claim. Scope: integer weights bounded by constant M; C_M depends on M.

label: S0010
statement: LEMMA S-P1-WIN (window form of Littlewood-Offord). Let a_1..a_k be nonzero integers and let W be a window of W consecutive integers {a, a+1, ..., a+W-1}. Then #{x in {0,1}^k : sum_i a_i x_i in W} <= ceil(W/2) * C(k, floor(k/2)); equivalently Pr_x[sum_i a_i x_i in W] <= ceil(W/2) * C(k, floor(k/2)) / 2^k. Proof: all |a_i| >= 1, so Erdős' 1945 Littlewood-Offord bound applies: every open interval of length 2 contains at most C(k, floor(k/2)) of the 2^k subset sums sum_i a_i x_i (assignments counted with multiplicity). For each pair of consecutive integers {b, b+1}, the open interval (b-1/2, b+3/2) has length 2 and contains exactly those two integers, hence at most C(k, floor(k/2)) assignments have sum b or b+1. A window of W integers partitions into floor(W/2) such pairs plus, if W is odd, one singleton; the singleton is bounded by the same interval-of-length-2 bound. Summing over the pairs gives ceil(W/2) * C(k, floor(k/2)). This fixes only the window-probability term in the bounded-weight restriction bound; it does not by itself close G0001/G0004/G0007/G0009, because the restriction count k <= C m L/sqrt(n) and the weight reduction from polynomial to bounded weights remain open.

label: S0013
statement: REPAIR (random thresholds). Let w in Z^n with |w_i| <= M, let c in Z be fixed, let S subset [n] contain each i independently with probability p, and let t be uniform on [-R, R] independent of S. Put mn = c + sum over i in S of min(w_i, 0) and mx = c + sum over i in S of max(w_i, 0). Claim: the gate y -> [c + sum_{i in S} w_i y_i >= t] on y in {0,1}^S is non-constant iff mn < t <= mx. Proof: the sum takes values in [mn, mx] and attains both endpoints; the gate is constant iff t <= mn (always 1) or t > mx (always 0). Given S, P_t(mn < t <= mx) <= (mx - mn)/(2R) because the interval has length mx - mn and t has density 1/(2R). Also mx - mn = sum over i in S of |w_i| <= M|S|. Taking expectation over S with E|S| = pn gives P(non-constant) <= M p n / (2R). With R = sqrt(n): P(non-constant) <= (M/2) p sqrt(n). This holds for every fixed c and every fixed x on the fixed variables, so it is an exact statement with constant M/2 and no assumption p <= 1/8.

structure.gap: The repair is for RANDOM thresholds only. It does not give H1 for the adversarial CTW gates, where the threshold is part of the circuit. The next step is to find a variant that keeps the thresholds fixed but takes x uniform on the fixed variables, and to prove an anticoncentration bound for the fixed-part sum (Erdos-Littlewood-Offord type) in that setting.

label: S0016
statement: CLAIMED (session R1023, unreviewed). Proof: the gate is non-constant iff Z = sum_{i in F} w_i x_i lies in the set of l consecutive integers {t-mx, ..., t-mn-1}, where mx, mn are the max and min of the alive sum. Erdos (1945): any open interval of length 2 contains at most binom(N, floor(N/2)) of the 2^N subset sums of N reals with |a_i| >= 1, so P(Z in open interval of length 2) <= binom(N,floor(N/2))/2^N <= 1/sqrt(N). Cover the l integers by ceil(l/2) blocks of at most 2 consecutive integers, each inside an open interval of length 2. Sum the bounds. Consequence: for gates with support >= 2n and L <= n/4 (so N >= n/4), P <= sqrt(2)(M/2+1) L/sqrt(n) for L >= 1.

structure.lemma: Fixed-threshold restriction lemma. Let w in Z^n with |w_i| <= M, t in Z fixed, S subset [n] with |S| = L, F = [n]\S, x uniform on {0,1}^F, and N = #{i in F : w_i != 0} >= 1. Let l = sum_{i in S}|w_i| <= ML. Then P_x[y -> [sum_{i in S} w_i y_i + sum_{i in F} w_i x_i >= t] is non-constant on {0,1}^S] <= (l/2 + 1)/sqrt(N) <= (ML/2 + 1)/sqrt(N).

label: S0017
statement: LEMMA (bounded integer weights, exact scope). Let w in Z^n with |w_i| <= M, let N be its support, s = |N|, and let t in Z be arbitrary. Each variable is alive (free) independently with probability p; each non-alive variable is fixed to an independent uniform bit z_i. Let g(x) = [w.x >= t]. Then E[ g is non-constant over the free variables ] <= (sqrt(2)*M + 2) * p * sqrt(s) <= (sqrt(2)*M + 2) * p * sqrt(n). PROOF. Fix the alive set A, let j = |A ∩ N|, b = s - j, and let c = sum over fixed i in N of w_i z_i. Put mx = sum over i in A of max(w_i,0), mn = sum over i in A of min(w_i,0), and W_A = mx - mn = sum over i in A of |w_i| <= M*j. Zero-weight variables affect neither c nor the window. g is non-constant iff mn + c < t <= mx + c, i.e. c in [t-mx, t-mn), a half-open interval containing exactly W_A integers. Since c is a uniform subset sum of b reals of absolute value >= 1: writing the signed sum as (sum a_i + sum eps_i a_i)/2 shows that an interval of length 1 in c is an open interval of length 2 in the signed sums. Erdos (1945) Littlewood-Offord then gives at most C(b, floor(b/2)) subsets per such interval. The W_A integers of the window give disjoint intervals (k-1/2, k+1/2), so #{subsets with c in the window} <= W_A * C(b, floor(b/2)). Using C(b, floor(b/2)) / 2^b <= 1/sqrt(b) for b >= 1, we get P(non-constant | A) <= min(1, W_A/sqrt(b)) whenever b >= 1; and P <= 1 always. AVERAGING. Case j <= s/2: then b >= s/2 >= 1 for s >= 2 (s = 1 with j = 0 has W_A = 0, probability 0). Here P(non-constant | A) <= M*j / sqrt(s/2) = sqrt(2)*M*j/sqrt(s), and E[j * 1{j <= s/2}] <= E[j] = p*s, so this case contributes at most sqrt(2)*M*p*sqrt(s). Case j > s/2 (this includes b = 0): by Markov P(j > s/2) <= E[j]/(s/2) = 2p, and P <= 1 contributes at most 2p. Summing: E <= (sqrt(2)*M + 2)*p*sqrt(s). QED. Scope: integer weights, |w_i| <= M, arbitrary threshold t, arbitrary n and p in [0,1]; the bound is per gate, so it also holds for the average over a family of gates.

label: S0018
statement: LEMMA (fixed threshold, exact scope). Let w in Z^n with |w_i| <= M, t in Z fixed, S subset [n] with |S| = L, F = [n] minus S, x uniform on {0,1}^F, N = #{i in F : w_i != 0} >= 1, and l = sum over i in S of |w_i| (so l <= M L). Then P_x[ y -> [sum_{S} w_i y_i + sum_{F} w_i x_i >= t] is non-constant on {0,1}^S ] <= l / sqrt(N) <= M L / sqrt(N). PROOF. Let mx = sum_S max(w_i,0), mn = sum_S min(w_i,0), so mx - mn = l, and let c(x) = sum_F w_i x_i. The map y -> sum_S w_i y_i has min mn and max mx. Hence the function is non-constant iff mn + c < t <= mx + c, i.e. c lies in the half-open window [t - mx, t - mn), which contains exactly l integers. Zero-weight variables in F do not affect c. Let a_1..a_N be the nonzero F-weights, |a_i| >= 1. For an integer k, c = k iff sum_i a_i(2x_i - 1) = 2k - sum_i a_i, so c in (k - 1/2, k + 1/2) is an open interval of length 2 for the signed sums sum_i a_i e_i with e_i in {+1,-1}. Erdos (1945) Littlewood-Offord gives at most C(N, floor(N/2)) sign vectors per such interval. Hence #{x : c = k} <= C(N, floor(N/2)) for each integer k, and the bad count is at most l * C(N, floor(N/2)). Dividing by 2^N and using C(N, floor(N/2))/2^N <= 1/sqrt(N) gives P <= l/sqrt(N). QED. Scope: integer weights, |w_i| <= M, arbitrary t, L, N >= 1. The bound l/sqrt(N) is proved; the sharper form (l/2 + 1)/sqrt(N) recorded in the lemma field is NOT proved here (only checked on exhaustive small cases with 0 violations: cm-363acd5f2b13434c, cm-71b683ac18654739).

label: S0019
statement: CLAIMED (session R1023, own proof, unreviewed). Let a = |S intersect supp(w)|, N = s - a. A gate is non-constant only if a >= 1. Given S, non-constancy means the fixed sum Z lies in l = sum over S of |w_i| <= M a consecutive integers. For each integer k, the subsets with sum k form an antichain after flipping signs (Sperner), so P(Z = k) <= binom(N, floor(N/2))/2^N <= 1/sqrt(N). Hence P_x[non-constant | S] <= M a / sqrt(N). Case s >= 2L: a <= L <= s/2, so N >= s/2 and P <= M a sqrt(2/s); E[a] = sL/n gives P <= sqrt2 M L sqrt(s)/n <= sqrt2 M L/sqrt(n). Case s < 2L: P <= E[a] = sL/n < 2L^2/n <= 2L/sqrt(n) <= 2ML/sqrt(n). Both cases give 2ML/sqrt(n).

label: S0033
statement: LEMMA (window count, nonzero integer weights; repair of S0011). Let k >= 1, a = (a_1..a_k) with every a_i in Z\{0}, and let W >= 1 be an integer. For any integer t, #{x in {0,1}^k : sum_i a_i x_i in [t, t+W-1]} <= W * C(k, floor(k/2)). PROOF. (1) Let P = {i : a_i > 0}, N = {i : a_i < 0}. Substitute y_i = x_i for i in P and y_i = 1 - x_i for i in N; this is a bijection of {0,1}^k. Since a_i x_i = a_i + |a_i| y_i for i in N, the sum equals C + sum_i |a_i| y_i for a constant C, so the count equals #{y : sum_i |a_i| y_i in [t', t'+W-1]} with t' = t - C. (2) Fix an integer v and let G_v = {J subset [k] : sum_{i in J} |a_i| = v}. If A is a proper subset of B and all |a_i| > 0, then sum_A < sum_B, so G_v is an antichain. By Sperner's theorem |G_v| <= C(k, floor(k/2)). The assignments y with sum |a_i| y_i = v correspond bijectively to G_v. (3) The window [t', t'+W-1] contains W integers, so the count is at most sum over those W values v of |G_v| <= W * C(k, floor(k/2)). QED. SCOPE: all weights nonzero. A zero weight multiplies the count by 2 and can be removed by factoring out 2^(#zero weights); for k' nonzero weights the bound then reads 2^(k-k') * W * C(k', floor(k'/2)). Verification: exhaustive over all a in {-3..3}\{0}^k, k<=5, W<=4, all integer t: 488,940 tests, 0 violations (cm-c2db9270a7c947aa); earlier independent random run cm-a4221c13235f4359, 245,528 trials, 0 violations. Control: the old bound ceil(W/2)*C(k,floor(k/2)) fails 7,722 times, as predicted. Status: bookkeeping for the window count. It does not close G0001, G0003 or G0004 and is not P vs NP progress.

label: S0001
statement: PROOF. (i) The Laplacian eigenvalues of the circulant on n=2k are 3 - 2cos(2pi j/n) - (-1)^j for j=0..n-1. j=0 gives 0. Odd j give 4 - 2cos(2pi j/n) >= 2. Even j != 0 give 2 - 2cos(2pi j/n), minimised at j=2 or j=n-2, with value 2 - 2cos(2pi/k) = 4 sin^2(pi/k) < 2. Hence lambda_2 = 4 sin^2(pi/k). (ii) Label u_i = i and v_i = i+k for 0 <= i <= k-1. Edges: rungs u_i v_i; rails u_i u_{i+1} and v_i v_{i+1} for i <= k-2; twisted edges u_{k-1} v_0 and v_{k-1} u_0. For k even take j = k/2 - 1 and S = {u_0..u_j, v_0..v_j}, |S| = k; the edges leaving S are u_j u_{j+1}, v_j v_{j+1}, u_{k-1} v_0, v_{k-1} u_0, so 4. For k odd take j = (k-3)/2 and S = {u_0..u_{j+1}, v_0..v_j}, |S| = 2j+3 = k; the edges leaving S are the rung u_{j+1} v_{j+1}, rails u_{j+1} u_{j+2} and v_j v_{j+1}, and the twisted edges u_{k-1} v_0 and v_{k-1} u_0, so 5. Hand checks: k=3, S={0,1,3} in Z_6 has 5 leaving edges; k=4, S={0,1,2,3} in Z_8 has 4.

(ii) There is S with |S| = k and exactly 4 edges leaving S when k is even, and exactly 5 when k is odd; so M2k has a balanced cut of width at most 5. label: S0004
statement: STATEMENT (restates S0015). G=(V,E), E = A disjoint-union B, D = V(A) cap V(B) nonempty, Ao = V(A)\V(B), Bo = V(B)\V(A); Sigma as defined in S0015. If G has a perfect matching M0 and vertex-disjoint M0-alternating cycles C_1..C_r, each containing an A-edge and a B-edge, then |Sigma| >= 2^r. PROOF. (1) For S subset of [r], M_S = M0 xor (union of C_i, i in S) is a perfect matching. a_S = M_S cap A covers Ao (every edge at an Ao-vertex is in A), so it is a valid row; b_S = M_S cap B covers Bo, so it is a valid column. (2) Each D-vertex is covered by exactly one M_S-edge, lying in A or in B, so sigma(b_S) = D minus sigma(a_S) and sigma(a_S) in Sigma. (3) For v in D let sigma_v(M) = 1 iff the M-edge at v lies in A. Vertices off the cycles keep their M0 value. For v on C_i, the M_S-edge at v is the M0-edge when i not in S and the other C_i-edge at v when i in S. Hence sigma(M_S) = sigma(M0) XOR (XOR over i in S of f_i) over GF(2), where f_i is the indicator of D-vertices on C_i whose two cycle edges have different labels. (4) C_i contains both an A-edge and a B-edge, so the cyclic label sequence changes at least twice; each change happens at a vertex incident to both an A-edge and a B-edge, i.e. a vertex of D on C_i. So f_i is nonzero. The supports of the f_i are disjoint (cycles are vertex-disjoint), so the f_i are GF(2)-linearly independent. Therefore S -> sigma(M_S) is injective on the 2^r subsets, all images lie in Sigma, and |Sigma| >= 2^r. QED. SCOPE: exact for any graph and any packing as stated. GAP: none found by hand check; the definition of Sigma is taken from S0015 and not re-read. STATUS: CLAIMED. Not reviewed. Authored in a claude-haiku-5-5 session, so it needs a SURVIVED_REVIEW from another model family. Evidence: cm-cbd09ec2d4ad44f4 (own code, n=6, 209 labelled graphs, 0 violations, min |Sigma| = 5 when r >= 2). That check is small (n = 6 only) and does not test n = 8 or larger.

label: S0005
statement: Switching bound (crossing form): let G be cubic bipartite with balanced cut (A,B), M0 a perfect matching, and C_1..C_r pairwise vertex-disjoint M0-alternating cycles, each containing at least one cut edge. For S subset of [r], let M_S = M0 xor (union of C_i for i in S) and sig(M) = M cap E(A,B). Then each M_S is a perfect matching, S -> sig(M_S) is injective, and |Sigma| >= 2^r. Proof: (1) flipping a vertex-disjoint alternating cycle preserves a perfect matching. (2) Let P_i = M0 cap E(C_i) cap E(A,B) and N_i = (E(C_i) minus M0) cap E(A,B). They are disjoint with nonempty union (C_i has a cut edge), so P_i != N_i. (3) By vertex-disjointness, sig(M_S) cap E(C_i) = N_i if i in S and P_i otherwise. (4) For S != S', pick i in the symmetric difference; the signatures differ on E(C_i) by (2). (5) Hence 2^r distinct signatures. Scope: cubic bipartite graphs, any balanced cut. Relation: weakens the S0015 side-changing hypothesis to 'cycle has a cut edge'.

label: S0001
statement: LEMMA (S-blowup-tw-identity, re-derivation, closes no obligation). For every finite graph G and integer d >= 1, let G[K_d] be the lexicographic product of G with K_d. Then tw(G[K_d]) = d(tw(G)+1) - 1. PROOF. Upper bound: take an optimal tree decomposition (T, {B_t}) of G of width k. Then (T, {B_t x [d]}) is a tree decomposition of G[K_d]: each bag has size d|B_t| <= d(k+1), every edge of G[K_d] lies inside some B_t x [d] because the copies of an adjacent pair are fully joined, and for each vertex (v, i) the nodes containing it form the same subtree T_v. Hence tw(G[K_d]) <= d(k+1) - 1. Lower bound: let (T, {B_t}) be any decomposition of G[K_d] of width w. For each vertex v of G let T_{v,i} (i in [d]) be the subtree of nodes containing copy (v,i). Copies of one vertex, and copies of two adjacent vertices, are pairwise adjacent in G[K_d], so every pair of their subtrees intersects. Subtrees of a tree have the Helly property, so all copies of v, and all copies of u and v for each edge uv, lie in a common node. Define B'_t = {v : all d copies of v lie in B_t}. Then (i) every edge uv of G lies in some B'_t, since u and v have all copies in a common bag; (ii) {t : v in B'_t} is the intersection of the d subtrees T_{v,i}, which is a nonempty subtree; so (T, {B'_t}) is a tree decomposition of G. Since the d copies of each vertex in B'_t are distinct vertices of B_t, d|B'_t| <= |B_t| <= w+1. So tw(G)+1 <= max_t |B'_t| <= (w+1)/d, i.e. w >= d(tw(G)+1) - 1. Both bounds together give equality. NOTE: this is the known fact that treewidth is multiplicative under clique blow-up; it is recorded for the manuscript's Lemma 10 check only.

statement:
statement: LEMMA (wiring-invariance of oracle circuits, sub-gap (iii)). Let C be a Boolean circuit with gates of fan-in at most beta, each gate either a fixed gate or an oracle gate with an arbitrary function of its inputs. Let W(C) be its wiring: the set of input-to-gate arcs and the input/output labels, with no gate functions. Let D(C) be the dependency digraph (vertices = inputs and gates, arc u->g iff u is an input of g). Then (a) D(C) depends only on W(C); (b) for any two oracle assignments O, O' on the same wiring, D(C_O) = D(C_O') as labelled digraphs; (c) any property P of digraphs closed under isomorphism satisfies P(D(C_O)) = P(D(C_O')) for all O, O'.
proof: (a) D(C) is defined from the arc set and the labels only; gate functions are not used. (b) Follows from (a), since equal wirings give equal labelled digraphs. (c) Equal labelled digraphs are isomorphic, so P agrees on them. QED. Consequence (the barrier test): if the width route proves a bound of the form S(C) >= phi(D(C)) for a function phi of the dependency digraph, then the bound holds for every oracle assignment on that wiring, which is the robustness property used by CHOPRS Thm 2 (B3-O). A bound that uses gate truth tables cannot be written as phi(D(C)). The identity of Thm 8 eq.22 and Lemma 10 eq.26 is a statement about the wiring of a fixed linear kernel: tw(D(K)) = tw(H_B). Replacing linear gates by oracle gates of fan-in <= N^eps changes the wiring (it removes the linear-overlap arcs), so the identity does not transfer by (a)-(c); this matches gap (ii).
scope: Pure definitional statement about wirings and dependency digraphs; no assumption on the kernel, on beta, or on the target (8). Holds for every finite circuit.
gap_left: G0001 (i) and (ii) remain open: the lemma does not bound S(C_m) by tw(H_B), and it does not decide whether the magnification upper-bound circuits share the kernel's wiring. The barrier status stays OPEN. Perfect-matching control and natural-measure test are still NOT CHECKED. This is a diagnostic reduction, not progress toward P vs NP; a reviewer should judge whether it discharges the barrier-test part of G0001.

label: S0002
statement: Proof of (a): a clause is falsified by x iff each of its literals is false, which fixes the variable of each literal to a specific value. Falsifying all clauses of S is the conjunction of these fixings. If two fixings give one variable different values, no x satisfies them, so |Fal(S)| = 0. Otherwise the fixings determine exactly |V(S)| variables and leave n - |V(S)| free, giving 2^(n-|V(S)|). A tautological clause forces some variable to both values, so it gives 0, consistent with its empty falsification event. Proof of (b): for each x, 1[x satisfies F] = prod over i of (1 - 1[C_i falsified by x]). Expanding the product gives sum over S of (-1)^|S| prod over i in S of 1[C_i falsified by x] = sum over S of (-1)^|S| 1[x in Fal(S)]. Summing over all x in {0,1}^n and using the definition of Fal(S) gives (b).

structure.lemma: Let F be a CNF over variables 1..n with clauses C_1..C_m (literals may repeat; tautological clauses allowed). For S subset of [m], let Fal(S) = {x in {0,1}^n : every clause in S is falsified by x}, and let V(S) be the set of variables occurring in clauses of S. Then (a) |Fal(S)| = 2^(n - |V(S)|) if no variable is forced to both values by the falsifying requirements of S, and |Fal(S)| = 0 otherwise; (b) #SAT(F) = sum over S subset of [m] of (-1)^|S| * |Fal(S)|.

label: S0013
statement:
statement: LEMMA (two-monomial Boolean hitting set). Let F be a field, t>=d>=1, and M=sum_{j=0}^d binom(t,j). There exists a set H of at most r=ceil(2^(d+1)(ln(M+binom(M,2))+1)) points in {0,1}^t such that every nonzero multilinear polynomial f over F with at most two monomials and degree at most d has f(a) != 0 for some a in H. Proof: Index monomials by supports S subseteq [t], |S|<=d; there are M supports. For each support S impose requirement A_S: some sampled point contains S. For each unordered distinct pair S,T impose requirement B_ST: some sampled point contains exactly one of S,T. For a uniformly random Boolean point a, A_S holds with probability 2^(-|S|)>=2^-d. For B_ST, choose an element in the symmetric difference, and name the supports so that it belongs to S\T. The event that every element of S is 1 and that chosen element of T\S is 0 has probability 2^(-|S|-1)>=2^(-d-1); it implies S is contained in a and T is not. Thus each requirement fails on one sample with probability at most 1-2^(-d-1), and on r independent samples with probability at most exp(-r*2^(-d-1)). There are M+binom(M,2) requirements. By the union bound, the probability any fails is at most (M+binom(M,2))*exp(-r*2^(-d-1))<=exp(-1)<1. So a sample satisfying all requirements exists; deleting duplicate points preserves satisfaction. For f=c*x_S with c!=0, A_S gives f(a)=c. For f=c*x_S+c'*x_T with distinct S,T and nonzero coefficients, B_ST gives a point where exactly one monomial evaluates to 1, so f(a) is c or c', nonzero over every field. Scope: existence only, multilinear degree<=d, at most two monomials; no polynomial-time construction claim or implication for general circuits. The size is O(2^d log M).

statement:
statement_start: LEMMA (degree-two multilinear Boolean hitting set). Let F be any field and t>=1.
statement: LEMMA (degree-two multilinear Boolean hitting set). Let F be any field and t>=1. Every nonzero multilinear polynomial p(x)=a_empty + sum_i a_i x_i + sum_{i<j} b_ij x_i x_j over F has a nonzero evaluation on H={0,e_i (1<=i<=t), e_i+e_j (1<=i<j<=t)}. Proof: If p vanishes at every point in H, evaluation at 0 gives a_empty=0. Evaluation at e_i then gives a_i=0 for each i. Evaluation at e_i+e_j gives a_empty+a_i+a_j+b_ij=0, hence b_ij=0 for every pair. Thus all coefficients vanish, contradicting that p is nonzero. Therefore H hits every nonzero polynomial in this class. Its size is 1+t+binom(t,2). The argument works in every characteristic. This is a bounded subclass result and gives no general circuit-PIT or P-vs-NP consequence.

statement: statement: LEMMA (sharp unrestricted linear case). Let F be any field and t>=1. The minimum cardinality of a set H subseteq {0,1}^t such that every nonzero multilinear polynomial f(x)=a_0+sum_{i=1}^t a_i x_i over F is nonzero at some point of H is exactly t+1. Upper bound: take H={0,e_1,...,e_t}; if f vanishes on H then f(0)=a_0=0 and f(e_i)=a_0+a_i=0, so each a_i=0. This is exact and constructive for degree at most 1 with unrestricted sparsity; it makes no PIT claim for general circuit classes.

statement: statement: LEMMA (minimum Boolean hitting-set size for unrestricted low-degree multilinear polynomials). Let F be any field, t>=1 and 0<=d<=t. Let V_{t,d} be the F-vector space spanned by monomials x_S=prod_{i in S}x_i for S subseteq [t], |S|<=d. Evaluation on the full Boolean cube is injective: if f vanishes on all points, its multilinear coefficients are recovered by Möbius inversion on the subset lattice, so f=0. statement: statement: For every field F and integers t,d,q>=1, let H={1_A in {0,1}^t: |A|<=min(qd,t)}. Every nonzero multilinear polynomial f in F[x_1,...,x_t] of degree at most d with at most q nonzero monomials is nonzero at some point of H. The restrictions of the distinct monomials x_{S_j} to {0,1}^U are linearly independent as functions over F: if their linear combination vanished at every Boolean point, then its multilinear polynomial would be the zero polynomial, by induction on |U| (write g=g_0+x_u g_1; evaluations at x_u=0 and 1 force g_0=g_1=0), contradicting at least one c_j!=0. Therefore some assignment a in {0,1}^U has f(a)!=0. Extend a by zeros on [t] minus U; its support A has size at most |U|<=min(qd,t), so the extended point belongs to H and still has f(a)!=0. The displayed size counts all subsets A of size at most min(qd,t). Scope is arbitrary fields, multilinear polynomials, degree at most d, sparsity at most q; this is an explicit enumeration, not a polynomial-time PIT guarantee when qd grows.

label: S0029
statement: LEMMA (bounded-sparsity Boolean witness). Let F be any field and let f in F[x_1,...,x_t] be a nonzero multilinear polynomial of degree at most d with at most q nonzero monomials. Then there exists a in {0,1}^t with Hamming weight at most min(qd,t) such that f(a) != 0. Proof: Let U be the union of the supports of the monomials of f. There are at most q supports and each has size at most d, so |U| <= min(qd,t). The polynomial f depends only on coordinates in U. A multilinear polynomial in |U| variables that vanishes on all Boolean inputs is identically zero: induct on |U|, writing f=g+x_i h; evaluations at x_i=0 imply g vanishes everywhere and hence g=0 by induction, while evaluations at x_i=1 then imply h vanishes everywhere and hence h=0. Since f is nonzero, some Boolean assignment to U has nonzero evaluation. Extend that assignment by zero outside U; its value remains nonzero and its weight is at most |U|. The full set of points of weight at most min(qd,t) is therefore an existential hitting set for this class, of size sum_{j=0}^{min(qd,t)} binom(t,j). This step is a bounded mathematical lemma, not a polynomial-time PIT algorithm and not a closure of the general-circuit PIT obligation.

statement: Let H={a^(1),...,a^(r)} be a set of Boolean points in {0,1}^t that hits every nonzero GF(2) multilinear polynomial with at most two monomials and degree at most d, where 0<=d<=t. Put M=sum_{j=0}^d binom(t,j). Then r>=ceil(log_2(M+1)).
evidence: For each support S with |S|<=d define its evaluation column v_S in GF(2)^r by v_S(k)=prod_{i in S}a_i^(k). The one-monomial polynomial x_S forces v_S != 0. For distinct supports S,T, x_S+x_T is a nonzero two-monomial polynomial over GF(2). If v_S=v_T, this polynomial evaluates to zero at every point of H, contradicting that H hits it. Thus the M columns are distinct nonzero vectors of GF(2)^r. There are only 2^r-1 such vectors, so M<=2^r-1 and r>=ceil(log_2(M+1)).

structure.lemma: K13-A(a). Let p be prime, q >= 2, T_q = {t in GF(p)^q : sum_i t_i = 0, t != 0}. Condition (L) for T_q: any two vectors of T_q have intersecting supports. Then (L) holds iff q = 3. Proof: (i) each t in T_q has |supp t| >= 2, since a single nonzero coordinate has nonzero sum. (ii) For q = 3, two vectors with disjoint supports would need >= 4 coordinates, but only 3 exist, so (L) holds. (iii) For q >= 4, t = e_1 - e_2 and s = e_3 - e_4 lie in T_q (sums are 0, entries are nonzero for every p >= 2) and have disjoint supports {1,2}, {3,4}, so (L) fails. Part (iii) is field-independent.

statement: LEMMA (dim-2 slice, tw=0): Let C subset GF(3)^n be a 2-dim code with no zero coordinate, G a 2 x n generator matrix with columns c_j. Then min over bases of tw(coefficient graph) = 0 iff the column matroid of G is disconnected. PROOF: edgeless coefficient graph for basis (u,v) iff supports of u,v are disjoint, i.e. each column has u_j=0 or v_j=0, so columns lie on the two points <e2>,<e1> of PG(1,3) and the matroid is a direct sum of two parallel classes (disconnected). Conversely, if nonzero columns use distinct points p,q of PG(1,3), a GL_2 change of basis maps p,q to e1,e2, giving disjoint supports. A simple rank-2 matroid with >=3 points is connected, so disconnection forces exactly two points. Scope: dim 2, no zero coordinate, tw=0 only. label: S0006
statement: REPAIRED LEMMA (any dimension k): Let C subset GF(3)^n be a k-dim code with no zero coordinate, with columns c_1..c_n of a generator matrix G (k x n). Then min over bases of C of tw(coefficient graph) = 0 iff the set of projective points {<c_j>} consists of exactly k points that form a basis of GF(3)^k (the matroid is a direct sum of k rank-1 parts). PROOF: For a basis, the coefficient graph is edgeless iff no coordinate j has two nonzero entries in the new basis, i.e. every column is a multiple of a basis vector e_r. Changing to such a basis is possible iff the columns' points are among k independent points p_1..p_k (take the change of basis g with g p_r = e_r). Rank k forces all k points to occur and to be independent. Conversely an edgeless graph on k vertices has tw 0 and any tw-0 graph is edgeless. Dim 2 case is the earlier lemma restated (2 independent points = disconnected rank-2 matroid with 2 points). Scope: all k, tw=0 only, GF(3). Closure: DERIVED from the definitions, elementary; novelty check still needed.

label: S0009
statement: LEMMA A (tw=0 characterisation, any k, GF(3)): for a code C of dimension k with no zero coordinate and generator columns c_j, min over bases B of tw(G_B) = 0 iff the projective points of the c_j are exactly k points forming a basis of GF(3)^k. PROOF: for a basis change A (rows of A G), column j has support T_j = supp(A c_j) and G_B is the union of cliques on the T_j. So G_B is edgeless iff |T_j| <= 1 for all j, i.e. every A c_j is a nonzero multiple of a unit vector; full rank k forces the k unit vectors to occur, so the points are k independent points. Conversely, such points are sent to unit vectors by A. LEMMA B (clique lower bound, any k): for every basis B, tw(G_B) >= max_j |T_j| - 1, since each T_j is a clique and tw(K_s) = s - 1 with tw monotone under subgraphs; hence min_B tw(G_B) >= min_A max_j |supp(A c_j)| - 1. Scope: GF(3), no zero coordinate, coefficient graph = rows adjacent iff supports share a coordinate.

statement: LEMMA T3 (k=3, GF(3)): Let G be a 3 x n generator matrix over GF(3) with no zero column and rank 3, S the set of projective points of its columns, and G_A the coefficient graph of rows of AG for A in GL(3,3) (rows adjacent iff supports share a coordinate). Then min_A tw(G_A) <= 1 iff S lies in the union of two distinct lines of PG(2,3). Proof: tw<=1 iff G_A not K3; a column with support size 3 forces K3; support size <=2 for all columns iff S lies in H_1 u H_2 u H_3 (the non-concurrent lines with normals = rows of A); the pair {r,s} occurs iff some point of S is private to H_t; so K3 iff every H_t has a private point. Two-line covers give tw<=1 via a third line M not through L cap L'; conversely no private point on H_t forces S in H_r u H_s. Consequence: min tw = 0 iff S is 3 independent points (234 sets), = 1 iff two-line cover, else = 2. Scope: k=3, GF(3). Does not close G0001.

label: S0018
statement: LEMMA U (upper bound, width theorem). Setting as in the owner lower-bound text (steps i-iv, S0009). Let (T,beta) be a tree decomposition of G of width k = tw(G). Let tau1 = (1,2,0) and tau2 = (0,1,2) in T (both sum to 0 mod 3; independent; their supports {1,2} and {2,3} meet in colour 2). For v in V and i in {1,2}, let b(v,i) in K_G be the element whose vertex part is tau_i at v and 0 elsewhere; its edge part is forced by k(e,c) = -(k(u,c)+k(w,c)). Restriction to vertex coordinates is an isomorphism K_G -> T^V, and the vertex parts of the b(v,i) form a basis of T^V, so B_T = (b(v,i)) is a basis of K_G. Support of b(v,i): coordinates (v,c) and (e,c) for edges e at v, with c in supp tau_i. Two basis vectors share a coordinate iff (a) they have the same vertex v (they share (v,2)), or (b) their vertices u,v are adjacent in G (they share (uv,c) for c in supp tau_i meet supp tau_j, nonempty by L2); nonadjacent distinct vertices share nothing. Hence H_{B_T} = G x K2 (strong product: each vertex blown up to a 2-clique, adjacent blocks fully joined). Tree decomposition of H_{B_T}: replace each bag beta(t) by beta(t) x {1,2}. Each (v,i) lies in exactly the nodes containing v (connected). An in-block edge lies in the bag of v. A cross edge (u,i)(v,j) with uv in E lies in some beta(t) containing u and v, hence in beta(t) x {1,2}. The width is at most 2(k+1)-1 = 2k+1. So min over bases of tw(H_B) <= 2tw(G)+1. With the owner lower bound (every basis has tw(H_B) >= 2tw(G)+1), w*(F(G)) = min_B tw(H_B) = 2tw(G)+1 exactly, relative to the spec's definition of tw(H_B). Status: CLAIMED, needs review by a session of a different model family. No barrier claim is made: this is a width fact about coefficient graphs of kernel bases; it is not a circuit or proof-size lower bound and does not transfer to P vs NP. Open: the earlier local-search note (tw(H_B) <= 2 when tw(G)=2) contradicts the lower bound and is being re-run with an independent encoding (see the verification experiment in this session).

statement: LEMMA H (upper bound, basis coefficient graph). Let G be a finite graph, k = tw(G), tau_1=(1,2,0), tau_2=(0,1,2) over GF(3)^3, and B_T = {b(v,i)} as in S0018 (vertex part tau_i at v; edge part -tau_i on edges at v). (a) The coefficient graph H_{B_T} equals the lexicographic product G[K_2]: vertex coordinates (v,c) are shared only by b(v,1),b(v,2), which share colour 1 since supp tau_1 and supp tau_2 both contain 1; edge coordinates (uv,c) are shared by b(u,i),b(v,j) iff c in supp tau_i and c in supp tau_j, which is nonempty for all i,j; no other shared coordinates. (b) Bag doubling: for an optimal tree decomposition (T,beta) of G of width k, beta'(x) = beta(x) x {1,2} is a tree decomposition of G[K_2]: bag size <= 2(k+1); the pairs (v,1),(v,2) lie together in any bag containing v; for uv in E the four pairs lie together in any bag containing u and v; for each (v,i) the bags containing it form the same subtree as for v. Hence tw(H_{B_T}) <= 2tw(G)+1. Scope: upper bound only, for the specific basis B_T; the equality min_B tw(H_B) = 2tw(G)+1 still needs the owner's lower bound (steps i-iv), which is not checked here. statement: For every finite simple graph G, tw(G[K_2]) = 2*tw(G)+1, where G[K_2] has vertex set V x {0,1} and (a,i)~(b,j) iff ab in E(G) or (a=b and i!=j). SCOPE: this is a statement about the fixed graph G[K_2] only. It does NOT bound min over bases of the coefficient graph of K_G, so it does not close G0001 or S0018.
derivation: UPPER BOUND: let (T,beta) be a tree decomposition of G of width k=tw(G). Set beta'(t)=beta(t) x {0,1}. Every edge (a,i)(b,j) of H has a=b (then a in beta(t) for some t, so both ends lie in beta'(t)) or ab in E (then a,b lie in a common bag). statement: LEMMA W-F (width theorem over an arbitrary field F). Let G=(V,E) be a finite simple graph, V nonempty, and let K_G^F subset F^I be the homogeneous kernel: (V) k(v,1)+k(v,2)+k(v,3)=0 for all v; (E) k(e,c)=-(k(u,c)+k(w,c)) for e={u,w}, all c. Then min over all bases B of K_G^F of tw(H_B) = 2 tw(G)+1, where H_B is the coefficient graph (j~k iff some coordinate is nonzero in both b_j and b_k). PROOF. Lower bound: the owner's Steps (i)-(iv) (LOWER_BOUND_PROOF.md, sec. 1) go through verbatim over F. The only arithmetic inputs are: (L1) T={t in F^3: t1+t2+t3=0} has dim 2, and every nonzero t in T has at least two nonzero entries, since a single nonzero entry cannot sum to 0; (L2) any two subsets of {1,2,3} of size >=2 intersect (2+2>3). Steps (i)-(iv) use only these, linear algebra, and Fact (C). Hence tw(H_B) >= 2 tw(G)+1 for every basis B. Upper bound: put tau1=(1,-1,0), tau2=(0,1,-1) in T. Both have supports {1,2},{2,3}, which meet only in colour 2 and both entries there are nonzero. They are independent (a*tau1+b*tau2=0 forces a=0 by coordinate 1 and b=0 by coordinate 3). For v in V, i in {1,2}, let b(v,i) have vertex part tau_i at v, zero at other vertices, and edge part forced by (E). Restriction to vertex coordinates is an isomorphism K_G^F -> T^V, so B_T={b(v,i)} is a basis. Coordinates of b(v,i): (v,c) for c in supp tau_i, and (e,c) for e at v with c in supp tau_i (the edge part of b(v,i) on e is -tau_i(c)). Then (v,i)~(u,j) in H_B iff u=v (common coordinate (v,2)) or uv in E (common coordinate (uv,2)). Non-adjacent distinct vertices share no coordinate, since an edge coordinate lies only on edges incident to the vertex. So H_B = G[K_2] (each vertex replaced by a pair, complete between pairs of adjacent vertices and inside each pair). For a tree decomposition (T,beta) of G of width k, the bags beta(t) x {1,2} form a tree decomposition of H_B of width 2(k+1)-1 = 2k+1. So min_B tw(H_B) <= 2 tw(G)+1. Together with the lower bound: min_B tw(H_B) = 2 tw(G)+1. SCOPE: any field F, finite simple G, the homogeneous 3-colour kernel only (not the affine solution set, not the non-linear two-value condition). ORIGIN: generalises the owner's GF(3) proof; the 'arbitrary-field version' of Q-fbfe10bfb3 is addressed here by hand. BARRIER CHECK: not a circuit or proof-system lower bound for P vs NP; no barrier analysis required. STATUS: CLAIMED, hand-checked by the claimant only (same family as the reviewers); novelty against Kashyap (0711.1383) and Hlinený-Whittle still open (Q-f0f8a3a9f1).

statement: Lemma F: min_B tw(G_B) = k-1 for the full projective point set. Upper bound: G_B has k vertices. Lower bound: column supports T_j are cliques (S0009 Lemma B), so tw >= max_j|T_j|-1. The point set is GL-invariant, so every basis has a full-support point; the k coordinate hyperplanes cover only points with a zero coordinate, and full-support points number 2^(k-1) >= 1. Hence some |T_j|=k, G_B contains K_k, and tw >= k-1. Scope: GF(3), one code family only.

label: S0025
statement: UPPER BOUND (claimed by claude-haiku-5-5 session, unreviewed). Setting: G=(V,E) finite simple, V nonempty, GF(3) homogeneous kernel K_G of the positive exact-one encoding with coordinates (v,c) and (e,c), c in {1,2,3}. Let tau_1=(1,2,0), tau_2=(0,1,2) in T (sum-zero vectors). Canonical basis B*: for v in V, i in {1,2}, b(v,i) has vertex entries tau_i(c) at (v,c), and edge entries -tau_i(c) at (e,c) for each edge e containing v, zero elsewhere. CLAIM: (1) each b(v,i) lies in K_G; (2) B* is a basis of K_G; (3) the coefficient graph H_{B*} equals G[K_2] (vertices (v,i), adjacent iff v=u with i!=j, or uv in E); (4) hence min over bases of tw(H_B) <= tw(G[K_2]) <= 2 tw(G)+1. PROOF. (1) Vertex sums of tau_i are 0. For e={v,w}: b(v,i)(e,c) = -tau_i(c) = -(b(v,i)(v,c)+b(v,i)(w,c)) since b(v,i)(w,c)=0; edges not containing v are zero on both sides. (2) Restriction to vertex coordinates is an isomorphism K_G -> T^V because edge entries are forced; dim K_G = 2|V|. Restrictions of b(v,1), b(v,2) are tau_1, tau_2 at v and 0 elsewhere; tau_1, tau_2 are independent in T (dim 2), so the 2|V| vectors span T^V and form a basis. (3) supp tau_1={1,2}, supp tau_2={2,3}; both contain colour 2. Same vertex v: share (v,2), adjacent. uv in E: b(v,i) and b(u,j) are both nonzero at (e,2), adjacent. Otherwise no coordinate is shared (vertex coordinates are only nonzero at their own vertex; edge coordinates only at endpoints). So H_{B*} = G[K_2]. (4) Take a width-tw(G) tree decomposition (T,beta); set beta'(t)=beta(t) x {1,2}. Edges (v,1)(v,2) lie in a bag containing v; edges (v,i)(u,j) with uv in E lie in a bag containing u and v. For each (v,i), the nodes containing it form a subtree (they are the nodes whose bags contain v). Max bag size is 2(tw(G)+1), so width <= 2tw(G)+1. QED.

label: S0001
statement:
statement_start: For every n>=1, threshold t, variable order, and level k, the OBDD width of f(x)=[sum_i x_i >= t] at level k is at most k+1.
proof: Fix the first k variables in the chosen order. For any assignment a to them, let j(a) be its number of 1s. On the remaining variables y, the residual is f_a(y)=[j(a)+sum_i y_i>=t]=[sum_i y_i>=t-j(a)]. Hence residuals are determined by j(a) in {0,...,k}; there are at most k+1 distinct residual functions, which is exactly the OBDD width at level k.

structure.gap: The result treats equal-weight thresholds only. The corrected gate question requires a lower bound or useful upper bound for explicit arbitrary-weight threshold functions, minimized over variable orders; no such result follows here.

label: S0002
statement:
statement_start: For every n>=1, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n<=W, integer threshold t, variable order, and level k, the OBDD width is at most kW+1.
statement: For every n>=1, nonnegative integer weights w_1,...,w_n<=W, integer threshold t, variable order, and level k in {0,...,n}, the Boolean threshold function f(x)=[sum_i w_i x_i >= t] has at most kW+1 distinct residual functions after fixing the first k variables in that order. Consequently its ordered binary decision diagram has size at most sum_{k=0}^n (kW+1)=W*n*(n+1)/2+n+1, hence polynomial size when W is polynomially bounded in n.
derivation: Fix a variable order and a level k. For any assignment alpha to the first k variables, let s(alpha) be the sum of w_i alpha_i over those variables. The residual on the remaining variables y is [sum_{i remaining} w_i y_i >= t-s(alpha)]. Since each fixed weight is an integer in [0,W], s(alpha) is an integer in [0,kW]. Thus there are at most kW+1 possible values of s(alpha), and assignments with the same value produce identical residual functions. The width at level k is therefore at most kW+1. Summing these width bounds over k=0,...,n gives the stated size bound. This argument covers zero weights and thresholds outside the attainable range as well.

statement: Lemma (Corrected Sparseness Bound): For every constant c >= 1, the number of truth tables on N = 2^n inputs computable by fan-in-2 circuits of size s = n^c is at most 2^{o(N)}. Proof: description length s*(4 + 2*log2(n+s)) + log2 s = 2s*log2(n+s) + O(s) = O(n^{c+1} log n) = o(2^n) = o(N).

label: S0005
statement: statement: Lemma (conditional deterministic-to-randomized inclusion). Fix an input length N and resource bounds T(N), S(N). Let K_det be a class of deterministic one-pass streaming machines for a fixed language L whose machines use at most T(N) time and S(N) space on every length-N input. Let K_rand contain randomized one-pass streaming machines under the same resource bounds, where deterministic behavior is allowed by ignoring the random tape. If a refuter R outputs, for every machine A in K_rand, an input y on which A errs (under the stipulated refuter quantifiers), then R also refutes every machine in K_det. Proof: For each A in K_det, define A' in K_rand with the same transition function and output, independent of its random tape. It uses the same resources and has identical output on every input, so any y witnessing error of A' witnesses error of A. This implication preserves the refuter's own uniformity and resources because R is unchanged. It applies only when K_det embeds with the same input-length indexing and resource bounds; it does not construct R or establish that K1 is contained in CJSW's resource-bounded class.

structure.gap: This conditional subclass lemma does not close G0001: the unresolved premise is whether every admissible K1 family satisfies CJSW's time/space bounds at matching lengths and whether the needed uniform constructive refuter exists. The resource match of Lemma 3.2 under its complexity assumption is not a K1 refuter.

label: S0006
statement:
statement: Residual-state lower bound. Let L be any language over {0,1}, let k be a cut position, and let R_k be the set of distinct suffix languages L_p={z : |z|=N-k and pz in L}, as p ranges over {0,1}^k. Every deterministic one-pass machine that decides L on length-N inputs must have at least |R_k| distinct states after reading k bits, and therefore at least ceil(log2 |R_k|) state bits. Proof: If prefixes p,p' with distinct residual languages reached the same state, there would be a suffix z accepted after one prefix and rejected after the other. Starting from the same state, the deterministic transition/output behavior on z is identical, contradicting correctness. Thus distinct residual languages require distinct states; taking logarithms gives the bit bound.
evidence: Direct proof by indistinguishable-state contradiction; applies to exact deterministic one-pass decision at a fixed length and cut. No K1-specific value of |R_k| is established, so this lemma does not prove the K1/CJSW resource match or close G0001.
